reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-three projected home runs from a 23-year-old third baseman is the kind of number that usually comes with a catch, and the catch here is in the bottom-right corner of the card: a 1st-percentile OAA. The bat profile is genuine — 93.0 mph average exit velocity at the 95th percentile, 50.2% hard-hit rate, and an xSLG of .493 that supports the projected .528 slugging without needing to imagine anything extra. His 18.4% strikeout rate is actually below the league median, and an 11.5% walk rate gives him the plate discipline foundation to let the power play at full volume across a 709-PA season. The whole profile hinges on Tampa deciding his bat is valuable enough to live with whatever the defensive metrics keep saying, but if they do, he's a middle-of-the-order force at a corner where that trade has been made for plenty of hitters far less talented.

The chase rate, 33.3%, is the one place pitchers can still attack him, and it's worth watching whether opponents start building entire plans around it. Add 30.1 ft/s sprint speed, a figure that almost nobody in the sport touches, and the projection's 43 stolen bases aren't a stretch, they're a floor dressed up as a ceiling.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The argument for Ohtani isn't a number — it's that two separate elite profiles happen to live in the same body. On the hitting side, a .401 xwOBA and 15.8% barrel rate describe a middle-of-the-order force; the one real tension is a 31.3% whiff rate that sits near the bottom of the league, which is why the projection lands at .278 rather than something wilder, and why his 13.3% walk rate does so much carrying. On the mound, a 2.73 xERA with a 30.4% whiff rate and only 3.8% barrels allowed isn't a curiosity; it's a genuine top-of-rotation profile, full stop. The whole read hinges on availability: if he pitches a full workload and reaches 691 projected plate appearances, there isn't a more valuable player on the field, and if the two-way strain clips either side, you're still holding a historically unusual asset, just a smaller one.

reports.name: Sal Stewart

The xwOBA sits at .350, which means the contact quality is translating, even if the hard-hit rate at 38.7% looks ordinary on the surface — he's barreling at a rate that outpaces how often he's just squaring things up. reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The contact-and-power profile looks like a middle-of-the-order bat; the plate discipline says he's not there yet. Walker's 92.6 mph average exit velocity and 13.5% barrel rate sit comfortably in the top tier of the league, and the .484 xSLG backs up the projection's .496 SLG without much squinting. The problem is a 35.9% chase rate and a 31.3% whiff rate that explain why all that raw thump is being taxed at the margins, keeping his BB% at 7.3% and his K% at 24.9%. If he tightens the zone enough to stop bleeding weak contact on pitches outside it, the 31 projected home runs and .837 OPS feel conservative; if he doesn't, he's a high-variance middle-of-the-order gamble who earns his counting stats through sheer force of contact quality rather than any patience buffer.

reports.name: Jackson Merrill
reports.published_report: The xSLG sits at .472 with hard-hit rate at 47.1%, and both numbers come from a hitter who is 23 years old and already logging full-season reps. reports.name: Eli Willits
reports.published_report: Ninety-two walks at age 18 in A-ball is not a coincidence — it's a skill, and it's the thing that makes the rest of this profile matter. The .405 OBP across A+ & A sits at the 91st percentile of his pool, and the 18% walk rate translates to 12.7% at the MLB level, roughly half again what most big-league hitters draw. The .192 ISO and 60 stolen bases across A+ & A tell you there's another gear: a teenager who draws walks, runs, and has started finding the pull side. If the contact sharpens and the ISO translates, he's an everyday shortstop; if the 25.7% MLB-equivalent strikeout rate hardens into a real liability, what's left is a very useful bench piece with plus plate discipline and wheels.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

reports.name: Corbin Carroll
reports.published_report: The tension in Carroll's profile is the gap between what the batted ball says and what the box score delivers. His 91.7 mph average exit velocity and 47.4% hard-hit rate are genuinely loud contact metrics, yet the xBA sits at .249, meaning he earns his value through quality rather than quantity of contact. The 11.6% walk rate is the glue, pulling the xwOBA to .343 even when the hit tool underperforms. Add 29.7 ft/s sprint speed and the profile becomes something pitchers can't fully contain: he converts walks into runs, weak singles into doubles, and steals 25 bases in a full season without needing a great average to do it. The whiff rate at 27.1% is the one lever that matters here — if it climbs further, the walk rate gets squeezed and the .810 OPS projection deflates quickly.

reports.name: Michael Harris II
reports.published_report: The xBA sitting at .289 in the 96th percentile is the crux: Harris makes such consistent hard contact, 48.6% hard-hit rate, that the batting average projection of .292 isn't optimistic — it's the floor that contact quality buys. The problem with the profile is naked on the Statcast card too, a 44.7% chase rate that puts him in the 2nd percentile and a 3.7% walk rate to match, which is why .321 OBP on .292 average is exactly what you'd expect from a guy who won't lay off anything but also won't miss much when he swings. If pitchers ever figure out how to exploit the aggression more systematically, the hit-rate magic dims and the OBP stays thin with no walks to cushion it; if they can't, you get 28 home runs and a .498 projected slug from someone who also grades at the 97th percentile in outfield defense. He's an impact regular whose ceiling is capped by his own plate discipline, not by his bat or his glove.

reports.name: Cam Schlittler
reports.published_report: 31.0 percent strikeouts, a 6.2 percent walk rate, and 98.0 mph on the fastball — the Statcast profile here isn't hiding anything. The spin backs the velo: 2532 rpm puts him in the top tier of fastball generators, and hitters are chasing at 33.9 percent while making meaningful contact only in spurts, with a .268 xwOBA and 2.97 xERA confirming the damage suppression is earned. The one honest tension in the profile is that his hard-hit and barrel numbers sit closer to the middle of the league, meaning he's winning on swing-and-miss and zone command rather than weak contact, so the profile holds as long as the fastball and the chase rate hold. If those do, the projection's 196.3 innings and 2.22 ERA start to look less like optimism and more like the floor.

reports.name: Walker Jenkins
reports.published_report: The contact rate is the headline: 15% strikeouts across AAA & A+ & A translates to 18.7% at the MLB level, well below where most big-league hitters land, and that's with a .237 ISO in tow. At 21, Walker Jenkins is posting a .417 OBP across those three levels while walking 43 times against only 50 strikeouts in 324 plate appearances, a combination that scouts get excited about precisely because disciplined hitters with real power don't usually need much fixing. The ISO translates to .171 at the MLB equivalent, above what most regulars produce, so the power isn't a minor-league mirage, but his ceiling as an everyday center fielder depends on how much of that contact quality survives a full diet of big-league velocity. If it doesn't hold, you're looking at a useful bench piece; if it does, the Twins have a true regular.

reports.name: Gunnar Henderson
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a riddle: 43.6% hard-hit rate but an xwOBA of .317, power that shows up in contact quality but somehow bleeds out before it reaches the expected slash line. The .243 xBA is the culprit — his batted-ball profile isn't generating hits at a rate that matches the exit velocity, which caps the ceiling even when he's squaring things up. The projection (.225/.308/.406, 26 HR in 718 PA) lands him as a solid everyday shortstop whose value lives in the counting stats and an 82nd-percentile glove, not in the slash line. If the hard-hit rate starts converting more consistently, there's a second-division-to-average regular in there; if the .243 xBA is the floor, what you see is basically what you're getting.

reports.name: Juan Soto
reports.published_report: A .422 xwOBA with a 17.0% walk rate is not a complicated profile — it's a case for one of the best offensive players in baseball, built on contact quality and plate discipline that almost no one touches. The chase rate sits at 20.2%, which puts him in rarefied company for a hitter who also barrels the ball at a 14.7% clip, and the .593 xSLG says the power is translating, not leaking. The projection (.280/.405/.541 across 474 PA) actually trails what the Statcast card implies, so the honest dependency is playing time: at full health, the floor here is a middle-of-the-order cornerstone; below 474 PA, you're pricing a smaller version of the same excellence.

reports.name: Paul Skenes
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 3.23 and the actual ERA projects to 3.84 — that gap is where the skepticism lives, but the Statcast profile says the run prevention is doing real work. A 28.9% strikeout rate with a 96.9 mph fastball gives him a floor most rotations would frame around, and the .279 xwOBA against tells you hitters aren't squaring him up even when they make contact. The one genuine lever: his 7.1% walk rate is the thing keeping the ceiling clipped, because a pitcher generating this much swing-and-miss at this velocity should be burying more counts than that. If the command tightens, the ERA closes toward that xERA and you're looking at a mid-to-upper-rotation anchor; if it doesn't, he's still a very good starter, just not the frontline kind.

reports.name: Jac Caglianone
reports.published_report: The contact quality is almost embarrassingly loud: 93.2 mph average exit velocity, a 54.6% hard-hit rate, and an xSLG of .507 all land in the top few percent of the league, and the .358 xwOBA says the underlying skill is outrunning whatever the surface line shows on a given day. The whole profile hinges on the chase rate. At 39.0%, pitchers will keep expanding the zone and daring him to swing at dirt, and a 29.3% whiff rate with a 6.0% walk rate tells you he's still biting often enough that this is a real disciplinary ceiling, not a rounding error. If he tightens the zone even modestly, the projection's .822 OPS probably undersells him; if he doesn't, he's a 27-homer bat who leaves meaningful value on the table every time a breaking ball lands a foot outside.

reports.name: Tyler Bremner
reports.published_report: The K-BB% is the number that carries this profile: 24% across AA & A+, which translates to a MLB-equivalent 14.6% when the level adjustment is applied. Bremner has struck out 92 batters in 68.3 innings while walking only 25, and that command-to-stuff ratio lands in the 96th percentile of his pitcher pool. If the walk rate holds anywhere near its current shape, he works as a back-end starter; if it softens, the strikeout rate still plays in a bullpen role.

reports.name: Luis García Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA and xSLG both sit at the 94th percentile, and a 16.5% strikeout rate is tame enough that the contact quality actually surfaces in results. García hits the ball hard, 91.7 mph average exit velocity, and does it often enough, at a 46.5% hard-hit rate, that a projected .540 SLG isn't a stretch. The problem is a 4.8% walk rate that pins OBP at .317, paired with a 38.6% chase rate that puts a ceiling on how much better the patience gets. If he keeps chasing at that clip, he's a power-over-OBP second baseman who runs into trouble against pitchers who stay off the zone; if the contact quality holds and he tightens the zone even a tick, the 31-homer projection reads as a floor rather than a ceiling.

reports.name: Rafael Devers
reports.published_report: The raw contact quality here is as loud as it gets, 93.0 mph average exit velocity with a 50.9% hard-hit rate, and those numbers belong to a genuine plus-power profile at the corner. The tension is the disconnect between that exit velo and a 29.1% whiff rate that drags his xBA down to .234, meaning the swing-and-miss keeps him from turning contact frequency into a true batting average threat. If the strikeout rate holds near 25.6%, Devers is an .840 OPS corner bat who gets to 37 home runs on sheer quality of contact; if pitchers find the holes more consistently, the floor is a thinner version of that same profile, just fewer plate appearances where the barrel matters. At 697 projected PA, the opportunity is full, and a .502 projected slugging says the power translates even against the contact limitations.

reports.name: Liam Doyle
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate jumps off the page, 11.5 K/9 at AA translating to 9.1 at the MLB level, but the walk rate is where this profile gets complicated. Fifty-two free passes in 98 innings at AA produces a BB/9 of 4.8, and the translation barely moves it, landing at 4.6 while the MLB average sits at 3.2. The K-BB% translates to 13.0 at the major-league level, right where the average falls, which is the quiet problem: elite strikeout stuff is being neutralized by the control, and nothing in this profile suggests the walks are an aberration rather than the shape of the pitcher. If the command sharpens, you have a rotation piece; if it doesn't, this is a depth arm cycling through the upper minors.

reports.name: Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact profile is quietly elite, and the projection ignores most of it. A 12.6% strikeout rate puts him among the sharpest contact men in the league, and his .282 xBA reflects that, yet the projection's .266 AVG and .377 SLG are well south of what his .401 xSLG says the contact quality should be producing. The disconnect lives in the barrel rate: 6.8% is ordinary, which means he's making exceptional contact without consistently elevating it for damage, and until that changes the power ceiling stays capped near the 12-home-run projection. If he starts lifting the ball at the same rate he makes it hard, the projection looks conservative by a wide margin; if the launch profile stays flat, .717 OPS is about right for a slow first baseman who puts the ball in play.

reports.name: Max Clark
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the lead. At AAA in 2026, Clark is punching out at 16% across 418 plate appearances — a number that translates to 18.7% against big-league pitching, well below a league average that sits around 22%. That's a contact profile you can build a lineup around, not a feel-good minor-league number propped up by inferior competition. The power is modest for now, a .157 ISO at AAA that translates to .134 against MLB arms, so the ceiling here is a patient, on-base-first center fielder with 21 stolen bases adding a wrinkle, not a middle-of-the-order bat. His 28.6 ft/s sprint speed is the translator, turning soft-side contact into hits that a slower player never sniffs, and it also explains how 21 projected steals sit comfortably alongside a .420 SLG projection. The walk rate at 7.2% is the number worth watching — if pitchers start burying him early and he stays passive, the whole offensive profile gets thinner fast. What's here now is a useful everyday outfielder with a real speed dimension, not a star, but a legitimate piece.

reports.name: Daylen Lile
reports.published_report: The contact quality is genuinely interesting here: an xSLG of .442 and an xBA of .261 from a 23-year-old who runs like a center fielder. He's getting to good results without elite raw contact, which usually means barrel placement and bat path are doing work that exit velocity isn't. The 38.2% chase rate is the real liability, and the 6.5% walk rate says he isn't making pitchers pay when he does lay off. At 29.3 ft/s sprint speed he's a weapon on the bases and in the outfield, and the projection's 16 steals across 660 plate appearances feels conservative if he stays healthy and in a lineup that lets him run.

reports.name: Pete Alonso
reports.published_report: The contact metrics and the power metrics are pointing in opposite directions, and that's the whole Alonso profile in a nutshell. His 94.3 mph average exit velocity and 57.3% hard-hit rate sit at the 99th percentile; his xSLG is .547, which is elite damage when he connects. The 24.1% strikeout rate is the cost of doing business — he swings through enough pitches that the projection settles at .266/.358/.499 rather than something scarier, and if that strikeout rate climbs further, the .857 OPS gets squeezed from the top. What's left if the contact side holds is a 38-homer, 107-RBI season from a guy whose underlying quality of contact is about as hard to argue with as any hitter in baseball.

reports.name: Chase Burns
reports.published_report: The 31.5% whiff rate and 35.1% chase rate tell you what Burns is: a pitcher who makes hitters swing and miss, not one who avoids hard contact when they do connect. The exit-velocity and hard-hit numbers sit right around league average, so when he leaves something over the plate, it gets hit. Everything rides on whether he can sharpen command — his walk rate sits at 8.4%, roughly league average, and that's the one lever that separates a 2.88 ERA projection from a guy who gives back leads in bunches. The 97.6 mph fastball with 2630 rpm spin is a genuine weapon that earns the strikeouts, and if the command tightens even modestly, he becomes a legitimate top-of-rotation piece; if it doesn't, the strikeouts keep him useful but the walks keep him from being great.

reports.name: Jamie Arnold
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the honest fault line in this profile. Across AAA & AA in 2026, Arnold has posted a 3.4 ERA over 118.3 innings with 130 strikeouts, but his 51 walks translate to a 4.0 BB/9 at the MLB-equivalent level, a figure that sits above where most big-league starters live, and his K-BB% translates to 11.8% when the MLB average is 13.5%. The stuff grades out fine, a 9.9 K/9 at these levels is workable, but the gap between what he strikes out and what he gives back for free is what keeps the ceiling from feeling like a lock. If the command tightens, he's a rotation piece; if it doesn't, he's a depth arm who eats innings until someone younger pushes him out.

reports.name: Ceddanne Rafaela
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here has one genuinely alarming number and one that almost explains the whole offensive game. A 45.4% chase rate sits at the 1st percentile, and the .282 xwOBA that follows from it is not a surprise, it's the consequence. What keeps this from being a disqualifying read is the sprint speed at 29.0 ft/s, a legitimate weapon that converts marginal contact into hits and inflates a .279 projection AVG well above what the xBA of .247 would suggest on its own. The Statcast contact metrics, 86.3 mph average exit velocity and a 31.8% hard-hit rate, say this is a guy who beats the ball into the ground or pulls the barrel through contact in ways that don't leave marks on a percentile card, and the 19 projected home runs feel like the optimistic end of a profile that generates most of its value through legs and defense, not the barrel. If the chase rate doesn't improve, the walk rate stays at 3.7% and the xwOBA stays in the basement, and what's left is a good-defender, speed-first outfielder who can be managed around in a lineup rather than built around.

reports.name: Hunter Goodman

A 16.1% barrel rate sits at the 98th percentile, and the .462 xSLG says the raw power translates even after you strip out Coors. At 6.0% BB%, he keeps hitters from reaching base freely, and a .271 xwOBA reflects a pitcher who suppresses contact quality well enough that the strikeout rate, a useful but not elite 25.4%, doesn't need to do all the heavy lifting. If the elbow holds through a full season, 14 wins and a 2.76 ERA is the floor, not the ceiling.

The problem is everything downstream: 87.2 mph average exit velocity and a 4.5% barrel rate mean the contact doesn't do much damage, and a .312 xwOBA tells you the bat plays closer to league-average than the batting average flatters. reports.name: William Contreras

Contreras makes enough contact, hits it hard enough (90.1 mph average exit velo, 43.5% hard-hit rate), and chases at just 28.1% to sustain a .261 xBA and .438 xSLG that both land well above the position's typical output. The projection lands at .272/.344/.407 across 651 PA, which reads conservative relative to the underlying Statcast profile — if the xSLG translates closer to reality, he's flirting with something better than that .751 OPS. The one real dependency is durability: he's a catcher projecting for a full workload, and everything here assumes he stays on the field.

reports.name: Spencer Torkelson
reports.published_report: Twelve-point-four percent barrels with a 31.2% strikeout rate is the whole contradiction in one sentence. Torkelson makes genuine contact quality when he connects, and his 22.0% chase rate is the discipline you'd expect from a high-bonus college bat, but a 31.3% whiff rate on pitches in the zone means pitchers have learned they can beat him without chasing him off the plate. The xBA sitting at .213 isn't a sequencing quirk, it's the contact quality splitting apart from the contact frequency in the worst possible direction for a first baseman who offers nothing on the bases. The 25-homer projection at .315 OBP is the profile of a low-end regular who stays in lineups mostly on the strength of the power, and that's exactly what he is unless the whiff rate comes down enough to let the barrel rate breathe.

reports.name: Cristopher Sánchez
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the engine here: 5.4% BB% puts him in rarefied air, and when you pair that with a 36.8% chase rate, you understand how a guy without top-tier velocity manufactures a 27.8% strikeout rate. reports.name: Wyatt Langford
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is quietly frustrating: a 9.9% walk rate, 27.7% chase rate, and legitimate speed, but the contact quality sits in the middle third of the league across every meaningful damage metric. His xBA is .240 and his xSLG is .392, which means the projection's .249/.333/.442 line is asking him to outperform what the ball-tracking actually sees in his swing. But if the contact quality doesn't climb, he's a second-division regular whose value lives on the margins, not in the box score.

reports.name: Luke Keaschall
reports.published_report: The contact and discipline profile is legitimate; the power is where the gap lives. Keaschall's 22.4% chase rate and 16.8% whiff rate put him among the better zone-managers in the league, but an 85.6 mph average exit velocity and 3.7% barrel rate say the contact is soft, and the .363 xSLG confirms there's no hidden pop waiting to emerge. The projection's .276/.367/.396 line reflects exactly that tension: a patient, fast, slap-contact type who posts 19 projected steals and walks at a 9.5% clip but won't beat you with the ball in the air. If the discipline holds and the legs stay healthy, he's a useful regular, the kind who contributes more to an OBP-friendly lineup than the .396 slugging suggests; if the soft contact gets attacked by pitchers who stop worrying about his chase numbers, there's a low-end starter who grades into a good-glove bench piece.

reports.name: Royce Lewis
reports.published_report: The barrel rate tells the most honest story here: 11.3% is genuinely loud contact, and the .410 xSLG bears it out, but a 32.7% whiff rate undercuts nearly everything else in the profile. Lewis hits the ball hard when he hits it, which is why the projection still lands at 17 home runs and 16 steals across 511 plate appearances, but the .239 AVG and .304 OBP are what a 24.7% strikeout rate costs you when it doesn't come paired with elite chase discipline — his 33.1% chase rate sits well below average. The whole profile hinges on whether he can get to that barrel rate consistently enough to offset contact losses, because if the whiff rate creeps further, the power upside compresses into a .714 OPS second-division regular with speed. A guy worth rostering, not one worth overpaying for.

reports.name: Andy Pages
reports.published_report: The xBA of .272 is doing real work here — his 88.8 mph average exit velocity sits below the middle of the pack, yet his expected batting numbers grade out well above it, which points to contact quality distributed into the gaps rather than loud, pull-heavy thunder. Pages hits the ball hard often enough (42.2% hard-hit rate) without being a true impact bat, and his chase rate of 31.6% explains why the walks haven't followed; he's a below-average draw man who still avoids the strikeout zone, which is a sustainable if narrow path. The projection's .271/.338/.458 with 22 home runs reads as a solid everyday outfielder with a little speed attached, and his fielding grades as an elite defensive asset at his position. That contact-over-power profile holds as long as pitchers don't find a lane to exploit his zone-expansion tendency, and if the chase rate climbs, the rest of the profile gets thin fast.

reports.name: Oneil Cruz
reports.published_report:
The contact rate is genuinely historic-bad, and it coexists with one of the most violent exit-velocity profiles in the sport.

Cruz's 95.3 mph average exit velocity is at the 100th percentile and his 17.2% barrel rate is at the 99th, which is how a 34.4% strikeout rate still produces an .xSLG of .484 and a projected .828 OPS. The walk rate at 11.7% keeps enough plate appearances alive that the power translates, and 30 projected steals mean his sprint speed (28.3 ft/s) compounds the damage when he does make contact. If he ever meaningfully cuts the whiff rate, you're talking about a perennial MVP candidate; if he stays where he is, you're talking about a legitimately weird, high-OPS, boom-or-bust middle-of-the-order piece who misses a third of the time and still hurts you.

reports.name: Masyn Winn
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile splits cleanly in two: elite plate discipline, no juice. Winn's 24.2% chase rate sits at the better end of the league, his strikeout and walk rates are right at the middle of the pack, and the contact itself is fine — a .248 xBA that lands exactly at the median. But a 3.6% barrel rate and 35.0% hard-hit rate are bottom-quartile power numbers, and the .333 xSLG confirms there's almost nothing to drive. The projection at .240/.315/.333 reflects that split honestly: a shortstop who won't beat himself, plays elite defense by OAA, and runs well at 28.4 ft/s, but whose offensive ceiling is constrained almost entirely by whether the bat-to-ball skills and speed can manufacture value that the raw contact quality won't. If the discipline holds and the legs age gracefully, he's a second-division regular who helps himself on the bases and never kills a lineup; if the power floor doesn't tick up at all as he matures, the profile slides toward a good-glove bench piece who starts against lefties.

reports.name: Trevor Rogers
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 3.76 while the projection calls for a 4.26 ERA, and that gap is the whole argument about what Rogers actually is right now. His chase rate tells you why the xERA is believable: 34.7% puts him in the 87th percentile, meaning hitters are expanding the zone against him at a rate most starters can't manufacture. The problem is that the swing-and-miss doesn't follow — a 23.7% whiff rate in the 38th percentile means he's getting bad decisions but not finishing them, which keeps the strikeout total modest across a full season and leaves the ERA exposed to sequencing. If the chase rate holds and the whiff rate climbs toward average, he's a mid-rotation piece eating 167 innings at an ERA that looks better than the projection; if the chases stay but the contact quality firms up even slightly, he's a back-end arm with good peripherals and a frustrating line.

reports.name: Seiya Suzuki
reports.published_report: The profile runs on plate discipline, and that discipline is genuinely exceptional: a 22.2% chase rate and 12.7% walk rate each sit in the 90th percentile, which is how a guy with an 88.4 mph average exit velocity and 38.5% hard-hit rate posts a .341 xwOBA. reports.name: Braylon Doughty
reports.published_report: The command-and-control case is louder than the strikeout case, and that's worth naming up front. Across AA & A+, Braylon Doughty has walked 23 batters in 99 innings, a 2.1 BB/9 that translates to roughly 2.7 against major-league competition, well below a league-average mark of 3.2. The strikeout rate tells a more modest story: 10.3 K/9 in the minors softens to about 8.1 equivalent at the big-league level, a tick short of average, which makes the 21% K-BB% across AA & A+ run almost entirely on the walk suppression rather than swing-and-miss. If that control holds as he climbs, a multi-inning or setup role is a real outcome; if the stuff doesn't miss enough bats at the highest level to keep the formula intact, what's left is a depth arm.

Cantillo generates whiffs on 29.7% of swings, a real separator, but a 28.3% chase rate means hitters aren't expanding the zone to get there, so the strikeouts are earned inside it, and the 11.7% walk rate is the bill that comes due. The xERA of 4.04 is the honest read on what he is right now; the 3.85 ERA projection implies some strand-rate luck holds, or that the 163.3-inning workload keeps him in enough low-leverage counts to cover the gaps. If the walk rate stays near double digits, this is a backend starter who gives Cleveland length but not margin.

reports.name: Brooks Brannon
reports.published_report: The power is the profile, and the profile has a ceiling problem. At AA, Brannon is hitting .286/.366/.572 across 373 plate appearances with 21 home runs, and the ISO of .286 translates to .194 against MLB pitching, in a league where the average sits at .15. The 29% strikeout rate at AA becomes 29.4% against the translation, and at first base with no defensive premium and a bench-or-depth floor, there's not a lot of margin for a swing that misses that often. If the power plays up and the strikeout rate softens even a little, he's a second-division regular; if neither budges, he's a roster filler who hits the ball very hard in Triple-A.

reports.name: Kendall George

The .424 BABIP will draw the side-eye, and it should, because the MLB-equivalent translation shows his ISO dropping to .092 while the MLB average sits at .150, meaning the whole offensive profile runs through contact and speed rather than power the ball doesn't have. If the bat-to-ball skill and legs translate, he's a low-end regular or a very useful bench piece with a specific gear; if the BABIP normalizes and the zero home runs across 278 PA stay zero, what's left is a depth outfielder who gets on base often enough to matter but not enough to hold a lineup spot.

reports.name: Max Meyer
reports.published_report: The 2614 rpm fastball spin is the whole engine here. Meyer's whiff rate sits at 28.6% and his K% at 26.2%, both comfortably above average, driven by a fastball that does unusual things at 95.1 mph because of that spin. The Statcast contact profile is the complication: an 8.6% barrel rate and 42.0% hard-hit rate suggest that when hitters do make contact, they're squaring it up, which is why the xERA of 3.86 is a full point higher than the projected 2.69 ERA. That gap is the bet ValuCast is making, that the strikeout shape and a WHIP of 1.14 across 112.0 projected innings will keep enough damage off the board, and it probably holds if the control (8.9% BB%) doesn't slip further.

reports.name: Vinnie Pasquantino

The projection's .723 OPS reflects that squeeze: the plate discipline is a genuine asset, the exit velocity at 89.7 mph just isn't the profile you need when your defensive value is close to zero and your sprint speed checks in at 25.7 ft/s. He's a second-division regular if the bat stays clean and the counting stats round up, and a useful bench piece if they don't.

His hard-hit rate sits at 32.4%, which is legitimately suppressed contact, with 86.9 mph average exit velocity putting him in the 85th percentile among pitchers, but his 21.3% strikeout rate and 9.5% walk rate are both below-average, meaning he's depending on weak contact rather than missing bats to sustain this. reports.published_report: The gap between what his batted-ball profile says he should hit and what actually shows up in the box score is the whole tension here. His xwOBA sits at .337 and his xSLG at .429, but a .212 projection AVG tells you the contact is landing wrong, and his xBA of .245 confirms the gap has shape to it. What keeps the profile from being a write-off is a 19.3% chase rate that ranks in the 98th percentile, meaning the walks (12.4% BB%) are the product of a guy who genuinely doesn't expand. reports.name: Bubba Chandler
reports.published_report: The fastball touches 98.4 mph and spins at 2405 rpm, which is a genuine weapon, and yet hitters are making contact at a 21.9% whiff rate that ranks in the bottom quarter of the league. That's the Chandler paradox: elite raw stuff, a 12.0% walk rate that bleeds away any advantage before he can press it. The barrel rate at 5.6% shows the heater does suppress damage when it's located, but a 4.12 xERA says the command problem is large enough to neutralize the stuff almost entirely. If the walks come down, he's a mid-rotation arm with real bite; if they don't, 155.2 innings of 4.32 ERA ball is the ceiling, not the floor.

reports.name: Griffin Jax
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a genuine puzzle: elite whiff and chase rates sitting directly on top of a contact-quality problem that doesn't go away. His 30.9% Whiff% and 34.8% Chase% both grade in the 88th percentile, but when hitters do make contact, a 9.2% Barrel% and 41.0% Hard-Hit% drag his xERA to 4.57 and his xwOBA to .328, both in the bottom quarter of the league. The projection at 3.78 ERA over 110.5 innings is banking on the swing-and-miss holding down the damage, and 2528 rpm on the fastball at the 96th percentile in spin is the reason the whiff rates are credible. If contact quality regresses even a turn, the gap between that projected ERA and the underlying contact metrics closes fast, and what's left is a backend arm with a good strikeout weapon and a profile that lives or dies by how often he can avoid the barrel entirely.

reports.name: Matt McLain
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a contradiction that doesn't resolve cleanly. His chase rate sits at 26.1% and his walk rate at 10.6%, both well above average, which says the zone judgment is genuinely there, and then a 28.3% whiff rate undercuts it, because he's making contact on bad pitches less often than he's laying off them. The barrel rate of 9.6% is fine, but 88.4 mph average exit velocity and a 37.1% hard-hit rate explain why the xBA clocks at .220: he's hitting the ball hard infrequently enough that the barrel count doesn't move the needle on actual production. If the strikeout rate, already at 27.4%, doesn't come down, the projection's .193 AVG across 519 PA is the honest destination, a useful speed and patience profile wrapped around a contact problem that leaves him as a below-average regular rather than the everyday shortstop Cincinnati thought they had.

If the strikeouts don't come down from 30.1%, he's a bench piece who walks and hits home runs in limited exposure; if he ever closes that whiff-to-barrel gap, the power is quietly real enough to matter.

reports.name: Ian Happ
reports.published_report:
The tension in Happ's profile is that gap between his walk rate and his strikeout rate. A 12.2% BB% is genuine plate patience, sitting well above average. But a 31.0% whiff rate undercuts it all, because he's making contact on so little of what he swings at, and the .204 xBA is the price: he can work a count and still not hit the ball where it needs to go.

The barrel rate at 11.3% is the saving grace, because when he does connect, it tends to count. That's enough to project 26 home runs over a full season despite the xBA sitting in the basement. What he is, plainly, is a three-true-outcomes corner outfielder whose .220 projected average reflects a real structural problem with contact, not a bad-luck stretch.

If the whiff rate plateaus where it is, he's a useful, slightly frustrating everyday player. If it climbs, the walks won't cover the shortfall.

The .931 OPS across AAA & AA turns heads, but the translation is what matters, and it's more complicated than the raw line suggests.

Across 437 plate appearances at AAA & AA, Luciano is hitting .298 with 24 home runs and a .251 ISO, and those translate to a .182 ISO against MLB pitching — meaningful pop, but not the kind that rewrites a ceiling. The strikeout rate at 26% in the minors translates to 26.3% in an MLB context, and that's the profile's hinge: if he can't trim it, the .361 BABIP driving that .298 won't travel and the hit tool thins out fast. The power is enough to sustain a bench role if the bat-to-ball holds; if the strikeout rate climbs against better stuff, what's left is a depth piece.

reports.name: Brandt Thompson
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one thing working in his favor, and it's not quite enough. Across AAA & AA this season, Thompson has posted a 3.7 BB/9 that translates to an MLB-equivalent 3.7 — tidy, but his strikeout rate translates to 8.4 K/9 while the average MLB arm sits at 8.6, and a K-BB% that comes out to 12.3% against a 13.5% baseline means he's not missing enough bats to carry the control advantage. He's worked 108.4 innings across those two levels with 117 strikeouts and 44 walks, so the shape is consistent and the sample is large enough to trust. If the walk control firms up and the strikeout rate creeps toward league norms, there's a back-end starter here; if neither moves, the depth arm floor is the honest ceiling.

reports.name: Johanfran Garcia
reports.published_report: The .290 average at AA is doing real work in this profile, but the strikeout and walk rates are pulling hard in opposite directions. At 21, Garcia is posting 18 home runs and a .503 slugging through 326 PA at AA, and the raw power translates to an MLB-equivalent .157 ISO, basically league-average pop at the next level. The problem is the contact-and-patience combination: a 29 K% against a 6 BB% in the minors converts to something close to 28.9% and 6.6% in an MLB environment, where average strikeout rate is 22.0% and average walk rate is 8.5%, which is a rough picture of a hitter who depends almost entirely on the ball finding grass to keep the batting average viable. If the .365 BABIP at AA compresses the way it usually does, the offensive case shrinks fast, and what's left is a right-handed catcher whose ceiling is organizational depth, not a roster fixture.

reports.name: Juan Brito
reports.published_report: The plate discipline is the whole résumé. At AAA in 2026, Juan Brito has drawn 64 walks against 84 strikeouts across 470 plate appearances, and that patience translates to an 11.3% walk rate at the MLB equivalent, ahead of what most big-league hitters post, while his translated strikeout rate of 20.1% is a tick better than the MLB norm. The problem is everything the walks are propping up: a .236 average with a .269 BABIP at AAA suggests there's no hidden contact luck being wasted, and the MLB-equivalent ISO of .127 is the quieter worry, sitting noticeably short of what a regular needs to profile as more than a bench piece. If the discipline holds at the next level, he's a bench bat with genuine on-base value; if pitchers hunt the zone and the bat speed doesn't answer, what's left is organizational depth.
